target_audience: Readers of revolutionary and devotional Bengali poetry
gist: A young poet strings a lute of fire and, through song, summons the sleeping masses of a colonized land to rise against bondage and claim their own dawn.
book_summary: Agnibeena (The Fiery Lyre) is Kazi Nazrul Islam's first poetry collection, published in October 1922. It burst onto a Bengali literary scene dominated by Tagore's serene mysticism with a raw, primal energy that challenged both the literary status quo and the British Raj. The twelve poems are distinct rhythmic weapons: Pralayollas opens with the ecstasy of destruction, Bidrohi proclaims the eternal rebel, and poems like Raktambor-Dharini Ma, Dhumketu, Kamal Pasha, Anwar, Qurbani, and Muharram fuse Hindu and Islamic imagery into a fierce secular humanism. The collection earned Nazrul his eternal moniker, the Bidrohi Kobi (Rebel Poet), and its poems were sung by freedom fighters during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War.

chapters.chapter_summary: The anthology opens with a chaotic, triumphant tone, urging the youth to welcome the destructive force of change that clears the path for a new dawn.

The crown jewel of the collection, written in a single night in December 1921. Through rapid-fire verses, Nazrul proclaims himself the eternal rebel who has risen beyond the universe, fusing Shiva's dance and Bhairava's wrath with Islamic motifs and universal humanism.

chapters.chapter_title: Raktambor-Dharini Ma (The Mother Clad in Blood)
chapters.chapter_summary: An ode to the fierce mother-goddess clad in blood, directly challenging colonial censorship and invoking the land as a wounded, waiting mother.
A poem of arrival and homecoming, weaving the devotional anticipation of the goddess's return with the longing for a free land.
A blazing comet of a poem that directly challenged colonial censorship, announcing the poet as a fiery omen of change streaking across the sky.
A celebration of the Turkish revolutionary Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, reflecting Nazrul's internationalist worldview and his salute to global anti-imperialist figures.
A tribute to the Egyptian nationalist Anwar Pasha, extending the poet's defiance beyond Bengal to the wider struggle against empire.
A martial poem beating the war drum of uprising, summoning the masses with a soldier's cadence to the field of struggle.
A poem named for the river of the Arab world, extending the poet's vision of a shared struggle across lands and waters.

chapters.chapter_title: Kheyaparer Tarani (The Ferry of the Far Shore)
chapters.chapter_summary: A lyrical meditation on crossing to the far shore, blending the ferryman's song with the soul's passage toward liberation.
A poem of sacrifice that weaponises spirituality against institutionalized religion, stripping away dogmatic divisions in the name of a shared offering.
The closing poem, an ode to the martyrdom of Karbala, uniting Hindu and Muslim youth under a single banner of defiance against oppression.

history: Agnibeena was published in October 1922 by a 23-year-old Kazi Nazrul Islam, a former soldier in the British Indian Army. It appeared amid the aftermath of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the waning Non-Cooperation Movement. The cover was designed by Abanindranath Tagore, and the book was dedicated to the revolutionary Barindra Kumar Ghosh. Several of Nazrul's subsequent works were banned and he was imprisoned for sedition, but the poems of Agnibeena were later sung by freedom fighters during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War.
